P13z2: Now, the Zapatistas also don't prove my whole economic path. (That's the one that goes from unpriced internal necessities, to a common purse, to getting rid of outside money.) Do their communities use collective work to support their schools and clinics, and their autonomous government and resistance? Yes. But they also sell products and trade, and they get outside support. What they do show is that major necessities and public functions can be taken out of ordinary market purchase and governed collectively. Outside help can make a community more capable, sure. But if the specialist or the donor or the organization stays indispensable, it can also create gatekeepers and uneven dependence.

P16e3: In the context of my research I have also looked for evidence of what happened after the Escuelita. While I found information on alumni networks, people bringing practices back with them, and organizing later, I couldn't find a clear chain of somebody having been to the Escuelita, then a new communal institution being set up, and then evidence about how its members and their children actually did over time. Zapatista influence was already spreading abroad before the Escuelita, so if some institution resembles a Zapatista one later, that alone doesn't prove the Escuelita was responsible. I'm borrowing the Zapatistas' teaching method and their ambition to replicate, not claiming they already proved my whole model.
P4f: Oventik itself was like something out of a dream. We played basketball outside with the Zapatista youth, and people gave us talks about their history and philosophy, which I translated for my friends because my Spanish was better. Visitors had come from all around the world to learn, and to make the communities less easy to attack in silence.
P5f: I felt a deep spirituality from them. I also suspect they may have a private relationship with ayahuasca, but nobody told me that, and it's only my impression, not something to take as fact.

Around 1,500 students came to the first sessions, and thousands more came to later ones.

P6g3: What impressed me most was how they do authority. They call it mandar obedeciendo, leading by obeying, which means the representatives carry the decisions people made in the assemblies, and they have to answer to the people who gave them the mandate.
P15h: One way an escuelita could fail is if it turns into a business, where the residents end up spending their lives performing community for outsiders who pay, and success gets measured by how many people show up instead of how many daughter communities get started. Giving people a week where they feel transformed isn't what it's for. It's for teaching enough of the social and material system that some of them can go build it somewhere else.
